pontificate

pon-TIF-ih-kayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To pontificate is to pompously express opinions.

Every Sunday dinner, Uncle Ray would pontificate about politics as though his opinion were simply beyond question.

Worked Example

At every family dinner, Grandpa would pontificate about the state of modern music as though no one could possibly disagree.

It wasn't just that he shared an opinion -- it was the pompous certainty and length of it, as if disagreement were unthinkable, that makes this pontificating.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lecture: To lecture someone is to talk at them in an instructive, often scolding way -- the point is to correct the listener's behavior or views. To pontificate is to parade your own opinions pompously, as though they were beyond question. A lecture aims at the listener; pontificating shows off the speaker.

hold forth: To hold forth is simply to speak at length about your views -- long-winded, perhaps, but not necessarily arrogant. Pontificating adds pomposity: the speaker acts as though disagreement were impossible. Anyone excited about a topic can hold forth; only the self-important pontificate.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defer: to yield to someone else's judgment

Where it sits · how overbearing the speech becomes — opine → pontificate → harangue

opine vs. pontificate: To opine is simply to state an opinion; to pontificate is to do so pompously, at length, as though the matter were settled.

harangue vs. pontificate: A harangue goes further than pontificating, turning a self-important opinion into a forceful, scolding speech aimed at its audience.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pontific

root — pontific: high priest (Latin (pontifex))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Pontific- (from pontifex, the Latin title for Rome's high priest) plus the verb-forming -ate gives 'to act the high priest' -- to pontificate is to talk as if you held that same unquestionable religious authority.

Use the root in a new word: pontiff

Use the root in a new word: pontiff: Pontiff is the modern English title drawn from the very same Latin word for a high priest, now used for the pope.

Word Choice

Pontificate is almost always critical -- it mocks the speaker's excessive self-importance. Compare it with opine, this unit's more neutral word for simply stating an opinion.
